responses.reason: The $214,000 ties out: 5,612,000 less 5,398,000, or -3.8%. S1 rests the whole seasonality argument on being consistent with the same month last year, and there is no prior year column in the table, so nothing supports it. Before I accept that driver I would need last July's distribution revenue and the school nutrition volume by depot on the page. I have seen neither.

The pair is S7 and S8. S7 says the depot repair program closed in June with no further repair spend expected this year, and S8 books $36,400 of July repairs as phase two of the Southline dock program. 118,600 less 36,400 is the $82,200 cited, so the amount is right. I believe S8, because cash actually moved and $36,400 is sitting on the ledger, which means S7 understates the remaining commitment and anyone forecasting off it will be short.

71,200 less 8,900 is $62,300, a 700 percent move, and the memo says nothing. Shrink of that size is either a physical loss, a count correction, or a plug covering an error in cost of product sold, and each of those is a different conversation. I would ask for the cycle count support by depot, the date the adjustment was posted, and whether it relates to July or is a catch-up for earlier months.

The defect is real but the challenge has framed it loosely. S10 already labels its percentage, so nothing is being mistaken for one. The problem is that the dollar figure is simply wrong: the account moved 74,900 to 76,300, which is $1,400, and 1.9 percent of 74,900 is $1,423, so $1,900 reconciles to neither. It should read that interest rose 1.9 percent, or $1,400, on the higher average revolver balance.

96,400 less 22,000 is $74,400, so the amount holds. S9 says the spend relates to a September trade show, which puts the benefit two months after the charge. The cost belongs in September when the show runs. In July the entry should have been a debit to prepaid expense and a credit to cash or accounts payable, with the release to account 6600 in September, and I want the invoices split between deposits and costs already consumed in July.

4,278,000 less 4,131,000 is the $147,000 cited. The driver S3 names, renegotiated inbound freight rates, affects account 5100 inbound freight, which fell $43,500 on its own line and which this memo's own definition excludes from cost of product sold. So the $147,000 is still unexplained, and the margin math says it is volume rather than rate: margin went from 23.8 percent to 23.5 percent, and cost fell 3.4 percent against revenue down 3.8 percent, so unit cost got worse, not better.

The cited amount does not exist. Warehouse wages went 702,500 to 781,900, a movement of $79,400, and neither balance nor the variance is $98,900, so I cannot tie $98,900 to account 6000 at all. S11 is also not a wages sentence; it is a claim about total operating expense as a share of revenue. The rounding criticism is fair on its own, and unrounded it fails: June opex of $1,080,100 on revenue of $6,774,000 is 15.9 percent and July opex of $1,180,400 on $6,622,500 is 17.8 percent, so the ratio rose about 190 basis points and even the rounded figures are 16 and 18, not 15. But that belongs to S11 and total opex, not to account 6000 and a figure I cannot reproduce.

The $7,500 is arithmetically right, 128,500 less 121,000, but the demand is not. This memo's stated rule requires commentary only when a movement exceeds both $25,000 and 10 percent, and at $7,500 and 6.2 percent this line clears neither gate, so requiring a driver contradicts the policy the memo is being tested against. The challenge also asserts that the account carried a reclassification last month, and nothing on the page supports that; there is no reclassification disclosed anywhere in the view. I will not sign a point that rests on a fact I have not been shown. There is a real question here, which is why billed freight rose while inbound freight cost fell $43,500, but that is a question about account 5100, not a threshold breach on 4200.

The amount is wrong. Service revenue went 1,041,000 to 1,096,000, which is $55,000, not the $38,000 cited, so the challenge is off by $17,000 before we get to its argument. The transfer theory is also unsupported: the challenge asks me to identify the other side of a reclassification, and there is no account in this table whose movement offsets $55,000 or $38,000 in the right direction. Distribution revenue fell $214,000 and freight billed rose $7,500, neither of which pairs with it. I am not going to invent a counterparty to make the challenge work.

62,000 less 9,500 is $52,500 and 52,500 divided by 62,000 is 84.7 percent, so the 85 percent holds. The memo is silent, and this is the movement I want explained most: bad debt collapsing while distribution revenue is falling suggests a reserve release rather than a genuine improvement in collections. I want the aging at both month ends, the reserve rollforward, and confirmation that no specific reserve was written back without a cash recovery behind it.

Fuel went 91,200 to 108,700, which is an increase of $17,500, or 19.2 percent. S4 says it declined, so the sign is reversed and the sentence tells the reader the opposite of what happened. Once corrected, the sentence also loses its own explanation, because diesel coming off a June peak cannot account for a cost that went up. The line needs a real driver, most likely July volume and the summer delivery schedule.

The difference is $4,500. The account moved $79,400 and S6 claims $74,900. I can see where the memo picked the figure up: $74,900 is the June balance of account 7100 interest expense, sitting a few rows down in the same table, so this looks like a copy from the wrong row rather than a transposition. Either way the overtime explanation is being sized against a number that is not the variance.

S5 puts roughly $9,800 of fuel consumed in the last week of July into August because that is when the invoice lands, and calling it normal practice does not make it right. The cost belongs in July. The entry should have been a July accrual, debit account 6100 fleet fuel $9,800 and credit accrued liabilities, reversing in August when the invoice posts. It matters beyond the amount: accrued, fuel is 118,500 against 91,200, a variance of $27,300 or 29.9 percent, which clears both the $25,000 and the 10 percent gate and makes this a line that requires commentary.
